newsitem.title: UK: Genetically engineered beer leaves ale lovers flat.
newsitem.headline: Genetically engineered beer leaves ale lovers flat.

text.p: Geneticists may have discovered a way to beat one of the most common problems to bedevil the world's drinkers -- stale beer.

Scientists at Carlsberg in Copenhagen have sucessfully delayed the onset of stale flavours by silencing a gene in a yeast the Danish brewer has used in making its beer since 1883, The New Scientist magazine reported on Thursday.
The scientists have made a yeast that releases six times as much sulphite into beer as normal yeast by silencing, or turning off, a gene that helps break down sulphites.
Sulphites prevent beer going stale by mopping up dissolved oxygen and other compounds that otherwise damage the flavour chemicals in beer.

"Staling of beer is a problem, and a lot of work goes into trying to control it," said Renton Righelato, the director-general of the British-based think-tank, Brewing Research Foundation International.
Carlsberg said it had no immediate plans to make beer commercially using the new strain of yeast.
A British group that lobbies for traditional beers was not certain there was any reason to froth over the genetic brew.

"Improving the life span of a product is not necessarily something consumers are worried about," said Steve Cox of the Campaign for Real Ale. "What they are more concerned about are the flavour and distinctiveness of the beer."
